title: A Normal Threshold Can Hide Damage

scenes.visual: Title card: A normal threshold can hide damage. Preview a cochlear synapse, gene replacement and the hair-cell regeneration barrier.

scenes.tts: A normal hearing test does not mean the cochlea is intact. In mice, hearing thresholds recovered after loud noise. Yet about half the ribbon synapses, the contacts that pass sound from hair cells to the auditory nerve, were lost at one place along the cochlea. A threshold tells us the quietest sound that gets a response. It does not count the synapses carrying the rest. That matters because recovered sensitivity can conceal injury. Repair then poses different problems: restoring release in surviving cells, or replacing hair cells that are lost.

scenes.visual: Lead with the finding, before the mouse details. A yellow hearing-threshold marker returns to its original height while about half the blue ribbon symbols become dashed outlines. Label the count as an illustrative sketch, not an individual cell measurement. End with two repair branches: restore release in surviving cells; replace lost hair cells.

scenes.tts: Kujawa and Liberman showed this in male C B A C a J mice. By two weeks after noise, thresholds were back to their old values. Hair cells remained intact. At eight weeks, ribbon counts at the thirty-two kilohertz place were about half of control. The cochlear nerve degenerated later.

scenes.visual: Retain the mouse timeline, with the strain and sex appearing as supporting context. Show threshold recovery and intact hair cells at two weeks, a ribbon-count bar about half of control at the 32 kHz place at eight weeks, and a separate later arrow for nerve degeneration. Do not depict neuronal loss as occurring at eight weeks.

scenes.tts: Human temporal bones also show auditory nerve fibre loss, worse with noise. But no one can count synapses in a living ear. Physiological proxies have uncertain sensitivity in people. A listening complaint alone does not establish the lesion.

scenes.visual: Replace the two proxy-study cards with a human temporal-bone evidence card and a separate living-ear diagnostic question. Solid evidence arrow for counted postmortem nerve fibres; dashed arrow from living-ear proxies toward an unknown synapse count. Distinguish nerve-fibre counts from synapse counts. Omit the SP/AP ratio comparison.

scenes.tts: Gene replacement has improved hearing in children with O T O F-related deafness. The missing activity sits in cells that survive. The otoferlin gene is too large for one conventional A A V vector. In mice, researchers split it across two vectors so cells receiving both could rebuild it. Human trials test hearing recovery separately. In the D B O T O trial, nine of twelve children met the week twenty-four endpoint: an average threshold of seventy decibels H L or better. Three reached average normal sensitivity. This treats O T O F-related deafness. Lifelong benefit remains unproven.
scenes.narration: Gene replacement has improved hearing in children with OTOF-related deafness. The missing activity sits in cells that survive. The otoferlin gene is too large for one conventional AAV vector. In mice, researchers split it across two vectors so cells receiving both could rebuild it. Human trials test hearing recovery separately. In the DB-OTO trial, 9 of 12 children met the week-24 endpoint: an average threshold of 70 dB HL or better. Three reached average normal sensitivity. This treats OTOF-related deafness. Lifelong benefit remains unproven.

scenes.visual: New treatment scene replacing the ceiling calculation. Begin with hearing recovery in children with OTOF-related deafness. Show a surviving inner hair cell and a mouse-labelled dual-AAV diagram: two gene portions enter the same cell and reconstitute full-length otoferlin. Transition to a separate human-trial card: DB-OTO, 9/12 at week 24, average threshold 70 dB HL or better; 3/12 average normal sensitivity. Keep genotype specificity and unproven lifelong durability visible. No percentage-of-hearing graphic.

scenes.tts: Birds show that hair-cell loss need not be permanent. They regrow auditory hair cells. Fish regrow hair cells in the lateral line, a different organ. Mature mammalian cochleas lack comparable spontaneous replacement. Mammals do have a vestibular exception: hair cells reappeared in guinea-pig utricles after damage. That is a different organ from the cochlea. Replacing lost cochlear hair cells remains an experimental repair goal.

scenes.visual: New regeneration scene. Compare bird auditory hair-cell replacement, fish lateral-line replacement and the mature mammalian cochlear barrier, with each species and organ clearly labelled. Add a separate guinea-pig utricle inset showing hair-cell reappearance after damage, labelled vestibular, not cochlear. End on lost cochlear hair-cell replacement as an experimental repair goal. Omit specific supporting-cell reprogramming experiments and do not depict restored mammalian cochlear hearing.

scenes.tts: What must a repaired synapse do? An inner hair cell releases transmitter onto auditory nerve fibres. Its ribbon helps keep vesicles in supply. Otoferlin is essential for release. In mice lacking it, exocytosis was almost abolished. Changing its calcium binding reduced the calcium sensitivity of release. That supports a calcium-sensing role, without showing it is the only sensor.

scenes.visual: Retain the inner-hair-cell, ribbon, vesicle-pool and auditory-nerve-terminal diagram as the final main-finding scene. Add two distinct mouse-evidence insets: otoferlin absent, release almost abolished; otoferlin present but calcium binding altered, calcium sensitivity of release reduced. Label essential for release and supports a calcium-sensing role. Do not label otoferlin the only calcium sensor or imply that ribbon supply alone restores hearing.
End card: normal thresholds can conceal synaptic injury; OTOF replacement can restore hearing in selected deafness; lost-hair-cell replacement remains experimental.
